title.purpose: Widget header name and consent client name. The most prominent type on a surface.

body.purpose: Row labels, grant copy, descriptions. The reading default.

label.purpose: Aisle/group headers and consent field labels — uppercase, quietly tracked.

mono.purpose: Reserved exclusively for the OAuth redirect host on the consent screen — the un-forgeable fact.

shadows.name: floating-toast
shadows.purpose: The widget toast overlaying the list. Negative spread keeps it a soft lift.

shadows.name: lifted-card
shadows.purpose: The consent card lifted a hair off the page — a tight contact plus a diffuse ambient layer, both warm and very low alpha.

motion.name: toast-in
motion.purpose: Toast entrance; fully disabled under prefers-reduced-motion.

motion.name: checkbox-fill
motion.purpose: Grocery checkbox filling to green on done.

motion.name: row-reorder
motion.purpose: A checked item sinking to the bottom of its aisle group. JS-driven slide/flip read prefers-reduced-motion explicitly, since Svelte JS transitions slip past the CSS reduced-motion block.

breakpoints.name: widget
breakpoints.purpose: Widgets fill the host's sandboxed iframe viewport; no fixed breakpoints — they flex to the pane the host gives them.

breakpoints.name: consent-card
breakpoints.purpose: The consent card's max-width; it centers on the page below that.

components.name: Ghost Button (Deny)

narrative.overview: The two HTML surfaces of the Paprika MCP Connector should feel like a well-run kitchen: competent, unhurried, and quietly trustworthy. Neither surface is a destination — both exist to let a person finish a thought and move on. The aesthetic is warm and food-forward but editorial, after NYT Cooking's warmth-with-restraint, never a bubbly consumer-recipe blog. Warmth is structural: every neutral carries a faint warm cast (hue ~72) so the surfaces sit native in a warm host. Color is rationed and always means something — a single paprika identity accent, a green for done/fresh, an amber for expiring, a red for danger. Depth is nearly absent: flat lists, hairline dividers, a shadow only on the one thing that genuinely floats. The voice is the OS system font, so a widget loads instantly in a sandboxed iframe and the consent page ships with zero web-font payload.
keyCharacteristics: Warm-neutral foundation (hue ~72) — paper, not gray; native inside a warm host.
One identity color (paprika), the rest semantic or neutral; color always carries meaning.
Host-matched typography — the widget adopts the shell's typeface (serif in a serif-first host, the host's sans otherwise) and ships no web font of its own.
Flat by default; one separator per category, and a shadow only on something genuinely floating.
Touch-native affordances (tap targets, swipe-with-fallback) borrowed from the OS, not invented.
Calm at the trust moment — legibility over alarm.

rules.name: The One Identity Color Rule
rules.body: Paprika is the only identity color on either surface. Everything else is neutral or a semantic signal. If a color isn't paprika and isn't carrying state, it's a warm neutral.

rules.name: The Two-Reds Rule
rules.body: Paprika-red is identity; alert-red is danger; they must never blur. The brand is one earthy paprika-red on every surface — it is not shifted or re-hued. Danger is a separate, vivid fire-engine red, deliberately more saturated, so the two warm reds stay legible apart where they share a view (a paprika brand tile in the header, an alert-red expired badge in a row). Brand and danger are never the same red.

rules.name: The Green-Means-Done Rule
rules.body: A completed or fresh state is always green, never a red checkmark. Done is a positive, and the color says so.

rules.name: The Match-the-Shell Rule
rules.body: A widget adopts the host's typeface, not its own — through the app SDK's style channel (--font-sans and the host's font CSS), a serif register for serif-first hosts and the host's sans otherwise, falling back to the system font. It ships no web font of its own; the security-critical consent page stays on the OS system font.

rules.name: The Mono-Anchor Rule
rules.body: The one element rendered in monospace is the OAuth redirect host — the single fact an attacker cannot forge. It gets the largest, most tamper-evident treatment on the screen. Nothing decorative borrows the mono face.

rules.name: The Flat-By-Default Rule
rules.body: Surfaces are flat at rest. A shadow is a signal that something is floating (the toast) or lifted off the page (the consent card) — never decoration on a resting list, row, or button.

dos: Do ration color: one paprika identity accent, plus green (done/fresh), amber (expiring), red (danger). If a color isn't paprika and isn't carrying state, make it a warm neutral.
Do keep paprika-red for identity (one earthy red, every surface) and a vivid fire-engine red for danger — distinct enough that they never blur where they share a view.
Do render done and fresh in green; a checkmark is satisfying, never a red 'done.'
Do match the shell's typeface via the host style channel (--font-sans / the host's font CSS); reserve monospace for the OAuth redirect host alone.
Do keep surfaces flat — hairline dividers and warm tonal shifts for separation; a shadow only on the toast and the consent card.
Do keep the warm cast on every neutral (hue ~72) so the surfaces sit native in a warm host.
Do borrow native affordances — real tap targets, swipe-to-act with a visible-button fallback — rather than inventing new ones.
Do keep the consent screen calm and legible: anchor on the redirect host, state the grant plainly, give Deny equal weight to Allow.
donts: Don't ship generic AI/SaaS dashboard slop — no gradient text, no tracked-uppercase eyebrows over every section, no identical icon-card grids, no glassmorphism, no hero-metric templates.
Don't drift into enterprise/admin-console heaviness — no gray-on-gray chrome, no heavy borders, no table-everything density where a calm list belongs.
Don't go cutesy consumer recipe app / food blog — no over-illustration, no bubbly-rounded everything, no emoji-heavy labels, no playful display fonts in UI. NYT Cooking, not a cutesy food blog.
Don't make the consent screen scary security-theater — no red warning banners, no fear copy, no phishy urgency. The redirect-approval earns trust by being legible and calm, never by shouting.
Don't use a cold or pure-gray neutral; paper is warm.
Don't add a shadow to a resting list, row, or button; flat is the default.
Don't ship a web font of your own to the widget iframe or the consent page — adopt the host's typeface instead.
Don't divide rows within a category with per-row hairlines — one full-width separator per category, never a line per item.
Don't blur the brand red and the danger red — keep the brand earthy and the alert vivid, never the same red in the same view.
